title: Network Delay Time
summary: A signal starts at node k; how long until every node receives it? That's the largest shortest-path distance from k. Dijkstra's algorithm pops the closest unsettled node from a min-heap and relaxes its outgoing edges.

complexity.note: Each edge can push one heap entry.

intuition: Weights are non-negative, so the closest unsettled node's distance is final.
Skip stale heap entries whose distance is larger than the recorded best.
Answer = max distance; if any node is unreachable, -1.
pitfalls: Forgetting to skip stale entries makes it slower (still correct).

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
summary: Connect all points with the least total Manhattan distance: a minimum spanning tree. Prim's algorithm grows the tree one point at a time, always adding the cheapest edge from the tree to a point outside it. On a dense graph, an O(n²) array version beats using a heap.

complexity.note: Every pair of points is a potential edge.

intuition: `dist[i]` = cheapest edge connecting point i to the tree so far.
Each round, add the outside point with the smallest dist.
Then update dist for the remaining points using the new point.
Kruskal with union-find also works, but needs all n² edges sorted.
pitfalls: Building all n² edges into a heap uses a lot of memory.
Using Euclidean instead of Manhattan distance.

def minCostConnectPoints(points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
    n, total = len(points), 0
    dist = [float("inf")] * n
    in_tree = [False] * n
    dist[0] = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        u = min((i for i in range(n) if not in_tree[i]), key=lambda i: dist[i])
        in_tree[u] = True
        total += dist[u]
        for v in range(n):
            d = abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0]) + abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1])
            if not in_tree[v] and d < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = d
    return total

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
summary: Find the cheapest flight from src to dst with at most k stops (k + 1 flights). Run Bellman-Ford for k + 1 rounds; each round relaxes every flight once, using a copy of the previous round's prices so a round adds at most one more flight.
intuition: After round i, `price[v]` is the cheapest cost using at most i flights.
Relax from the previous round's copy, or a round could chain several flights.
Plain Dijkstra fails because a cheaper path may use too many stops.
pitfalls: Updating prices in place lets one round use multiple flights.
Treating k as the number of flights instead of stops.

title: Path With Minimum Effort
summary: A path's effort is its largest height difference between consecutive cells; find the path with the smallest effort. Dijkstra works with "cost = max edge so far" instead of a sum: always expand the cell with the smallest effort to reach it.

complexity.note: Each cell can be pushed a few times.

intuition: `effort[r][c]` = the smallest maximum step needed to reach (r, c).
Moving to a neighbour costs `max(effort, |height difference|)`.
The first time the bottom-right is popped, its effort is final.
Binary search on the answer plus BFS is an alternative.
pitfalls: Summing differences instead of taking the max.
Stopping when the target is first pushed rather than first popped.

title: Swim in Rising Water
summary: At time t you can swim through cells with height ≤ t. Find the earliest time to reach the bottom-right. The answer is the smallest possible maximum height along a path, so expand cells in order of height with a min-heap, tracking the highest cell seen.
intuition: A path is usable at time t exactly when its highest cell is ≤ t.
Always expand the lowest reachable cell next (min-heap by height).
The time needed so far is the largest height popped.
Stop when the target is popped.
pitfalls: Forgetting that the start cell's own height counts.
